sub: One Cadence brain (cadence-net 0.91.1) playing Super Mario Bros. World 1-1 from the screen. One brain, trained once and kept learning, not a seed average.
lede: A Cadence brain learned to play the first level of Super Mario Bros. from the screen alone, overnight, on one desktop PC. On its own its best round runs, jumps Goombas and clears pipes to x 1,783, more than half of World 1-1 (random buttons die around x 594). With a coach that steps in only after a death it reaches the flag on every start that finished, pressing 59-69% of the buttons itself. Six rounds earlier it managed 41%. It does not yet clear 1-1 unaided, and its solo distance swings a lot from round to round. Both replays below are real NES frames.
seeing:
The real NES game, recorded frame by frame from the emulator. Two clips: brain alone (every button pressed by the Cadence brain, no help at all, ending where it dies) and full level, assisted (the brain plays, and after each death or stall the game rewinds about a second and the coach drives briefly; the badge turns red while the coach drives). The lit keys are what was held for each 4-frame decision. The bar is how far into the level Mario is.

The brain does not see the game the way you do. It gets a 26 x 32 grid of grey blocks (each block averages 8 x 8 pixels) for the present moment and for one decision ago, with the sky subtracted so only things light up. That is 1,664 numbers. It does not get Mario's position, the enemies' positions, or anything from the game's memory.
how:
1. Watch a coach. The coach is not a learner: at every moment it saves the emulator, tries 17 short button plans (run, run-jumps of different heights, wait, back off), and keeps the first button of whichever plan ends furthest right without dying. It clears 1-1 from every start we tried. The brain watched it play 20 times, some of them with deliberately wrong buttons mixed in so it also saw how to recover.
  2. Learn the screens. Each watched moment is one labelled screen. The brain learns them in shuffled lessons of 32 screens through Cadence's own local learning rule (equilibrium settling plus a nudge toward the shown button), at the library's teaching="normalized" point for imitation, with learning_surprise=True so it only studies the screens it still gets wrong. No backprop.
  3. Play, get corrected, repeat (DAgger). The brain plays on its own. Its own buttons are executed, so it reaches places the coach never went (like standing in front of a Goomba it should have jumped). The coach labels every screen the brain reached, the labels join the pile, and the same brain keeps learning. Some attempts start from a random point along the coach's path, so the brain also practises the later parts of the level. This is the recipe in Cadence's own teach guide.
  4. Test. After every round the brain plays alone from 5 fixed starts (0 to 23 idle frames before the first button, which shifts every Goomba's timing). That is the curve above.
caveats:
• It learned from a coach, not from the score. Every label came from the look-ahead coach, and the coach cheats in ways the brain cannot: it reads Mario's position and the death flag from the game's memory and tries plans in saved copies of the emulator. The brain only ever sees the grey blocks. This is imitation (DAgger), not reinforcement learning.
  • One level, one brain. It was trained and tested on World 1-1 only. The level is the same every time; the only variation is the 0-23 idle frames at the start, which shift when the Goombas arrive. So some of what it knows is surely "this screen means jump" for this level, not Mario in general. It has never seen 1-2.
  • Hand-made input. I chose the view: 8 x 8 grey blocks with the sky subtracted. With raw pixels on the bright sky, every Cadence setting I tried gave the same button for every screen (sweep in mario/sweep.py). That preprocessing is my design, not something the brain learned.
  • Not the full Cadence recipe. The brain plays with predict: its settled network answers each moment on its own, without the working trace or episodic memory the library also offers. Cadence's own roadmap (#118) calls this kind of frame-to-button imitation a component, not the continuing world-model brain it is aiming for.
  • The assisted run is assisted. In the full-level replay the coach takes over after every death or stall (marked COACH DRIVING in red, with the game rewound a few seconds first). The share of buttons the brain pressed is printed under it. The "brain alone" replay has no help at all, and it ends where the brain died or got stuck.
  • It went wrong three times before this. Raw grey pixels with 7 buttons: the brain just held run. Colour blocks: its answer swung between "always run" and "always jump". And for the first 7 rounds of this run, a bug made the test attempts use an old copy of the brain, so those measurements were thrown out and re-measured from saved checkpoints (the curve shows only re-measured or post-fix points). Details in mario/PROGRESS.md.
  • The MLP row is a cheap reference. It is trained on the brain's final pile of labelled screens with backprop, so it gets the benefit of all the brain's DAgger rounds for free. It is not a matched rival.
doom: Sean heard someone made Cadence play Doom. What we found: Doom is on Cadence's official roadmap as issue #118, "Build and qualify the full native Doom expert", an open epic whose first skill is ViZDoom's Basic combat room, with only rendered screen information allowed into the player. We found no posted Cadence Doom results or public demo. The issue also says that a frame-to-action classifier taught by a host planner is a component control, not the full expert it is after. That is a fair description of this Mario demo too: it shows how far that component gets, nothing more.
chart_note: Each grey dot is one start, the orange line the median. Rounds 3 and 6 are re-measured from saved checkpoints; rounds 7 on are live. Round 8 is the peak (median 1,417). After it the brain wobbles between about 300 and 725: more DAgger rounds kept adding labels without making it steadier. That plateau is the main open problem.
note_replay: Round 8 brain, start 0, no help. It gets past the first Goombas, the pipes and the first pit, and dies at x 1,783 of 3,161.
note_assist: Round 10 brain, start 11. The brain pressed 69% of the buttons; the coach stepped in 7 times. Red badge = coach driving.
assist_intro: The same brain (round 10, the best saved checkpoint by median) playing all of 1-1 from each start, rescued by the coach after every death or stall. For comparison, the round-4 brain needed 13 rescues on start 0 and pressed only 41% of the buttons. Start 17's assisted run did not finish (it kept needing rescues at one spot) and was stopped.
